title: Sampling-method comparison (LHS, Sobol, random): which sampling covers better?
summary: Three ways to choose the same number of sample points in a two-dimensional parameter space: purely random, Latin hypercube and Sobol. The panels show the points; the discrepancy under each says how evenly they cover the square.

media.alt: Three square scatter plots in a row, each with 64 points on a unit square with faint gridlines: random (rose circles, clumps and gaps, discrepancy 0.0073), Latin hypercube (blue squares, more even, 0.0004) and Sobol (teal triangles, most even, 0.0002).
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.4 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which sampling covers better?
read_the_figure.axes: Each panel: x1 on the horizontal and x2 on the vertical axis, both 0 to 1 and with equal aspect; the y axis is shared. Gridlines at every eighth. The discrepancy of each design is printed under its panel.
look_at: Which design has clumps and empty patches? Count the empty cells of the grid.
Do the designs have the same number of points (the same cost)?
How different are the discrepancy values, and is a lower value better?
Would a different random draw look different? (One realisation of a random design is shown.)
as_drawn: Three designs of 64 points: random (rose circles), Latin hypercube (blue squares) and Sobol (teal triangles), identical axes and the same n written in the footnote.
The random panel has visible clumps and empty patches; discrepancy 0.0073. The Latin hypercube is more even (0.0004). The Sobol design is the most regular (0.0002).
On the 8 by 8 grid a random design of 64 points leaves about 23 of the 64 cells empty on average; a Latin hypercube leaves about 20 empty; a Sobol design leaves none.
Only one realisation of each random design is shown, and the discrepancy is for that draw only.
read_the_figure.proves: At equal n, a lower discrepancy means the points cover the square more evenly, so integrals over the square are estimated with smaller error. It does not tell you how any particular function behaves.
if_wrong: Different n in the panels: the comparison is not like for like. The class requires the same n.
A single random draw taken to represent all random designs: repeat and average.
A Sobol design with n not a power of two: the balance properties are lost.
must_check: same n: a design with more points always covers better, so the comparison is only fair at equal n.

terms.meaning: Independent uniform draws; clumps and gaps arise by chance.
A design with exactly one point in each of the n equal strips of every coordinate.
A deterministic low-discrepancy sequence; with n = 2^m points it fills elementary boxes equally.
A number measuring how far the empirical distribution of the points is from the uniform distribution; smaller means more even.
Integration using low-discrepancy points; the error decays almost like 1/n instead of 1/sqrt(n).
How evenly points fill the space, as seen in empty cells and clumps.

remember: Random: error of an integral falls as n^(-1/2).
Low-discrepancy: error falls almost as n^(-1) (up to log factors).
A Latin hypercube is one point per strip in each coordinate, but not necessarily even jointly.
Random leaves about n (1 - 1/n)^n of n cells empty, 36 percent.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each panel shows the same unit square with 64 points; colour and marker shape distinguish the three methods so the plot survives greyscale. Faint gridlines at every eighth let the eye count points per cell. The number under each panel is the discrepancy of the displayed point set. The note at the bottom states the equal n and how to read the number.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if you throw 64 darts at a square, some places are crowded and some empty; a better design spreads them out. Looking at the three squares shows this immediately, and the number gives it a size. For estimating an average over the square, evenly spread points waste less effort, because two points close together tell you nearly the same thing.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Two dimensions are friendly: in many dimensions the advantages shrink and projections hide holes. One random draw can be lucky or unlucky; the stated discrepancy is for that draw. A Latin hypercube is even in each coordinate, but it can still clump jointly (about 20 empty cells here against 23 for random), which its low discrepancy number hides. And a low-discrepancy set is not random: no error bar for the estimate comes from it directly.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A table of the root-mean-square error of an integral estimate against n for each design shows the benefit directly. The parameter coverage matrix (F7.8) shows all pairs for a higher-dimensional design. Randomised (scrambled) Sobol points restore error estimates by repetition.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Repeat each design 100 times and show the discrepancy as a box plot, add a fourth panel with a regular grid of 8 by 8, and plot the integration error of a test function against n for each design.

steps.title: Monte Carlo error
steps.note: The Koksma-Hlawka bound: the error of a low-discrepancy estimate is at most the variation of the function times the star discrepancy.

steps.title: A numerical check
steps.note: The root-mean-square error of the n-point mean over 100 repeats: random 0.038 (n = 64) and 0.0096 (n = 1024), a factor 4 for 16 times the points; scrambled Sobol 0.0017 and 4.1e-5, a factor 42.

steps.title: Empty cells of a random design
steps.note: About 36 percent of the cells; the Sobol design has none because its 2-D projections form a net.

worked.title: Reading the sampling comparison of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) By what factor is the discrepancy of the Sobol design lower than that of the random design? (2) How many of the 64 grid cells would you expect to be empty for the random design, and what does the picture show? (3) How does the error of an integral scale with n for the random and the Sobol design?

solution.text: (2) The expected number of empty cells for random points.
The random panel indeed shows about a third of its cells empty, with clumps in others.
(3) From the check above, 16 times more points cut the random error by 4 (1 / sqrt(16)) but the Sobol error by about 42.

worked.answer: A factor of about 36 in discrepancy; about 23 empty cells expected for random points; random error falls as n^(-1/2) (factor 4 for 16 times the points) and scrambled Sobol error roughly as n^(-1.35) (factor 42).

analyze.q: The Latin hypercube has a low discrepancy yet leaves about 20 of 64 cells empty. Is that a contradiction?
analyze.hint: One point per strip is a property of each coordinate, not of pairs.

analyze.q: Why would you not use a Sobol set of 100 points?
Why does the advantage of low-discrepancy points shrink in many dimensions?

evaluate.q: You want an uncertainty estimate for your integral. Is plain Sobol a good choice?
evaluate.hint: Deterministic points give no variance estimate; scrambling and repeats do.

create: Repeat each design 100 times and show the discrepancy as box plots; add a regular 8 by 8 grid as a fourth panel.
Plot the integration error of e^(xy) against n for the three designs on log-log axes.

checks.q: Why compare the designs at the same n?
checks.answer: More points always cover better; only at equal n (equal cost) does the comparison show the effect of the design.

checks.q: A random design puts 100 points in 100 equal cells. How many cells are empty on average?
A Latin hypercube looks more even than random in each coordinate but still has clumps in the plane. Explain.
checks.answer: It guarantees one point per strip in each coordinate separately, not in each cell of the pairwise grid; the points can still pair up badly, so joint coverage is only partly improved.
